prompt: Why is economics described as a social science?

options.label: A
options.text: It can test every theory in a controlled laboratory.

options.label: B
options.text: It avoids the use of evidence about human decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: It studies human behaviour and choices in society.

options.label: D
options.text: It studies only physical laws that do not change.

explanation: Economics is a social science because it studies how people, firms and governments behave and make choices within society. Human behaviour and institutions are central to the subject, even though economists also use data, models and quantitative methods.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement is positive?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment rose from 4% to 6% last year.

options.label: B
options.text: A fair economy should have substantially lower unemployment.

options.label: C
options.text: The current unemployment rate is morally unacceptable.

options.label: D
options.text: Employment should take priority over controlling inflation.

explanation: A positive statement is factual or testable and does not depend on a value judgement. A recorded change from 4% to 6% can be checked against evidence, whereas 'unacceptably', 'should' and 'fair' express judgements.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is meant by ceteris paribus?

options.label: A
options.text: All economic variables must increase together.

options.label: B
options.text: Only long-run changes can be considered.

options.label: C
options.text: Every assumption in an economic model is known to be true.

options.label: D
options.text: Other relevant things are assumed to remain unchanged.

explanation: Ceteris paribus means 'other things remaining equal'. Economists use the assumption to isolate the effect of one change while holding other relevant influences constant.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which description best fits the short run?

options.label: A
options.text: All factor inputs and all other key conditions can be changed.

options.label: B
options.text: A fixed number of months has passed in every industry.

options.label: C
options.text: Some, but not all, factor inputs can be changed.

options.label: D
options.text: No factor input can be changed.

explanation: In the short run a firm can vary some inputs but not all of them. The short run is therefore defined by what can be changed, not by a universal calendar length.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which feature of economics most directly reflects its status as a social science?

options.label: A
options.text: Evidence is restricted to controlled laboratory observations.

options.label: B
options.text: Expectations have no influence on observed outcomes.

options.label: C
options.text: People’s decisions help determine observed economic outcomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Predictions follow immutable laws of physical behaviour.

explanation: Economics studies choices and behaviour by individuals, firms and governments. Because people can respond differently as circumstances and expectations change, economic relationships are not mechanical physical laws.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement is normative?

options.label: A
options.text: Inequality should fall even at the cost of higher taxes.

options.label: B
options.text: The top income-tax rate rose by five percentage points.

options.label: C
options.text: Measured income inequality rose during the previous calendar year.

options.label: D
options.text: Tax records show an increase in total income-tax receipts.

explanation: The word 'should' introduces a value judgement about what ought to happen. The other statements are factual or testable claims and are therefore positive.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economist changes one variable in a model and assumes all other relevant influences are unchanged. Which methodological device is being used?

options.label: A
options.text: The very long run

options.label: B
options.text: A laboratory control group

options.label: C
options.text: A normative judgement

options.label: D
options.text: Ceteris paribus

explanation: The economist is applying ceteris paribus by isolating one change and assuming that other relevant determinants remain constant. This makes a complex relationship easier to analyse.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which description best fits the long run?

options.label: A
options.text: The period must last at least one year.

options.label: B
options.text: All factor inputs can be varied.

options.label: C
options.text: Only labour can be varied.

options.label: D
options.text: Technology and government regulation must also have changed.

explanation: In the long run all factors of production are variable. The definition does not depend on a fixed number of months or years, and changes in wider key conditions are associated with the very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why is it often difficult for economists to conduct controlled experiments on an entire economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Several influences on behaviour can change together.

options.label: B
options.text: Economic data cannot include numerical observations.

options.label: C
options.text: Economic theories cannot incorporate simplifying assumptions.

options.label: D
options.text: Social science cannot use observations as evidence.

explanation: An economy involves many people, institutions and variables that cannot usually be held fixed while only one influence is changed. This makes laboratory-style control difficult and is one reason economists rely heavily on models, observations and other empirical evidence.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt:
The table contains three statements about an economy. Which classification is correct?
| Statement | Text |
| 1 | Consumer prices rose by 3% last year. |
| 2 | A 3% inflation rate is too high. |
| 3 | The central bank raised its policy interest rate. |

options.label: A
options.text: Statement 1 is positive, statement 2 is positive, and statement 3 is normative.

options.label: B
options.text: 1 positive, 2 normative, 3 positive

options.label: C
options.text: 1 normative, 2 normative, 3 positive

options.label: D
options.text: 1 normative, 2 positive, 3 positive

explanation: Statements 1 and 3 can be checked against data, so they are positive. Statement 2 uses 'too high', which is a value judgement about what the inflation rate ought to be, so it is normative.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A researcher wants to examine the effect of a change in household income on spending. Why might the researcher assume other determinants of spending are unchanged?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the analysis apply only in the very long run

options.label: B
options.text: To prove that household behaviour never changes

options.label: C
options.text: To turn a normative statement into a positive one

options.label: D
options.text: To isolate the effect of the income change

explanation: Holding other determinants constant is a ceteris paribus assumption. It allows the researcher to attribute the change being analysed to income rather than to several simultaneous influences.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which description best fits the very long run?

options.label: A
options.text: Inputs, technology and other key conditions can vary.

options.label: B
options.text: Only labour can vary while other inputs stay fixed.

options.label: C
options.text: Inputs can vary but technology must remain fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: Inputs stay fixed after exactly ten calendar years.

explanation: In the very long run not only are factor inputs variable, but wider key influences such as technology, government regulation and social considerations may also change. There is no universal calendar duration.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why do economists use simplified models?

options.label: A
options.text: To make forecasts certain under every possible condition.

options.label: B
options.text: To convert judgements of fairness into observable facts.

options.label: C
options.text: To isolate important relationships within a complex economy.

options.label: D
options.text: To replace the need to compare predictions with evidence.

explanation: Economic reality contains many interacting influences. A model simplifies that reality so economists can focus on particular relationships and reason about them, while recognising that assumptions can limit how closely the model matches the real world.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is a positive economic statement?

options.label: A
options.text: A lower sales tax would be a better policy.

options.label: B
options.text: The sales tax is unfair to low-income households.

options.label: C
options.text: A 2% sales tax was introduced on 1 January.

options.label: D
options.text: The sales tax should be abolished immediately.

explanation: The date and rate of a tax are factual claims that can be verified. The other options contain judgements about fairness, what should happen or which policy is better.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economist estimates the effect of a change in bus fares on the number of bus journeys. Which assumption best represents ceteris paribus?

options.label: A
options.text: Bus fares are assumed never to change again.

options.label: B
options.text: Other determinants of bus travel are held constant.

options.label: C
options.text: All transport prices are assumed to change by the same percentage.

options.label: D
options.text: The estimate is treated as a value judgement.

explanation: Ceteris paribus requires other relevant determinants to be held constant so the effect of the fare change can be isolated. It does not mean that variables are permanently fixed in reality.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A bakery can alter workers' hours next week but cannot change the size of its premises. Which time period is being described?

options.label: A
options.text: The very long run

options.label: B
options.text: The short run

options.label: C
options.text: A period that cannot be classified

options.label: D
options.text: The long run

explanation: The bakery can change some inputs but not all of them because its premises remain fixed. This is the defining feature of the short run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is the role of empirical evidence in economics?

options.label: A
options.text: To make every person’s behaviour perfectly predictable.

options.label: B
options.text: To identify fairness without any value judgements.

options.label: C
options.text: To remove every assumption from economic theories.

options.label: D
options.text: To test positive claims against observed outcomes.

explanation: Empirical evidence consists of observed or measured information and can be used to examine positive economic claims. Evidence cannot by itself settle value judgements such as what is fairest or most desirable.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement contains a value judgement?

options.label: A
options.text: Public transport fares rose by 8%.

options.label: B
options.text: The average fare is $3.20.

options.label: C
options.text: Passenger numbers fell after fares increased.

options.label: D
options.text: Public transport fares are excessively high.

explanation: Calling fares 'excessively high' requires a judgement about what level is acceptable. The other statements can in principle be checked against observed data.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which phrase has the same methodological meaning as ceteris paribus?

options.label: A
options.text: Other things remaining equal

options.label: B
options.text: Assuming the conclusion is correct

options.label: C
options.text: Over a fixed period of one year

options.label: D
options.text: After all variables have changed

explanation: Ceteris paribus is the Latin expression used by economists for 'other things remaining equal' or 'other relevant things held constant'.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why can the short run be six months for one firm but a different length for another firm?

options.label: A
options.text: The time needed to change all factor inputs differs between firms.

options.label: B
options.text: The long run begins only when prices stop changing.

options.label: C
options.text: The short run is chosen according to whether a statement is normative.

options.label: D
options.text: Every firm uses a different definition of ceteris paribus.

explanation: Economic time periods are defined by the ability to adjust inputs, not by a fixed calendar duration. Different firms and industries can therefore reach the long run after different amounts of clock time.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economist predicts that a policy will change household behaviour. Why is the prediction not necessarily a physical-law certainty?

options.label: A
options.text: Economic predictions cannot contain any theoretical reasoning.

options.label: B
options.text: Human responses vary with circumstances and expectations.

options.label: C
options.text: Social-science predictions cannot use observed economic evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Positive forecasts express judgements about desirable outcomes.

explanation: Economics studies people and institutions, so responses can depend on changing circumstances, incentives and expectations. Economic theory can identify likely relationships without making every outcome mechanically certain.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A report states: 'A congestion charge reduced traffic by 6%, and the city was right to introduce it.' How should the statement be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: It is entirely normative because it mentions policy.

options.label: B
options.text: It contains both a positive claim and a normative judgement.

options.label: C
options.text: It is neither positive nor normative because two ideas are combined.

options.label: D
options.text: It is entirely positive because it includes a percentage.

explanation: The 6% traffic reduction is a testable positive claim. Saying the city was 'right' to introduce the charge is a value judgement, so the full statement contains both positive and normative elements.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A manufacturer is able to change the quantities of all its factor inputs when planning a new production process. Which time period is relevant?

options.label: A
options.text: A fixed three-month period

options.label: B
options.text: The short run

options.label: C
options.text: The very long run only

options.label: D
options.text: The long run

explanation: When all factor inputs can be varied, the firm is in the long run. The very long run additionally allows wider key influences, such as technology or regulation, to change.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement can be positive even though it is a forecast rather than an observed fact?

options.label: A
options.text: The proposed tax increase would be morally wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: The government ought to protect every household’s income.

options.label: C
options.text: The tax increase will reduce disposable income next year.

options.label: D
options.text: A reduction in disposable income would be unacceptable.

explanation: A positive statement is one that is testable in principle; it need not describe only past events. A forecast about a measurable 2% change can later be compared with evidence, whereas the other options contain value judgements.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What does economics mainly investigate as a social science?

options.label: A
options.text: Choices made by people and organisations.

options.label: B
options.text: Motion of objects independent of human behaviour.

options.label: C
options.text: Moral judgements without any factual investigation.

options.label: D
options.text: Chemical reactions under controlled laboratory conditions.

explanation: Economics studies how individuals, firms, governments and other organisations make choices and interact. This human and institutional subject matter is why it is classified as a social science.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which comment on the tax system expresses a value judgement?

options.label: A
options.text: The income-tax rate increased by two percentage points.

options.label: B
options.text: Unequal tax shares are unfair to some households.

options.label: C
options.text: Some households pay one-fifth of their income in tax.

options.label: D
options.text: Income-tax receipts reached twelve billion dollars last year.

explanation: The judgement that an outcome is 'unfair' depends on values and cannot be established by measurement alone. The other options are testable factual claims.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which row correctly distinguishes the short run from the long run?

options.label: A
options.text: Short run: all inputs variable; long run: no inputs variable.

options.label: B
options.text: Short run: some inputs fixed; long run: all inputs variable.

options.label: C
options.text: Short run: all inputs fixed; long run: only labour variable.

options.label: D
options.text: Short run: technology variable; long run: all inputs fixed.

explanation: The short run is characterised by at least one factor input remaining fixed, while in the long run all factor inputs can be varied. Calendar length alone does not define either period.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt:
Two statements are shown. Which classification is correct?
| Statement | Text |
| P | A 5% rise in fares will reduce rail journeys. |
| Q | The government should prevent rail fares from rising. |

options.label: A
options.text: P positive; Q positive

options.label: B
options.text: P normative; Q normative

options.label: C
options.text: P normative; Q positive

options.label: D
options.text: P positive; Q normative

explanation: Statement P predicts a measurable consequence and is therefore testable in principle. Statement Q says what the government should do and therefore contains a value judgement.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A survey finds that two groups respond differently to the same price change. What does this most clearly illustrate about economics as a social science?

options.label: A
options.text: Behaviour can vary across people and contexts.

options.label: B
options.text: Calendar length alone determines an economic time period.

options.label: C
options.text: Positive claims cannot be tested using observed data.

options.label: D
options.text: Models cannot include any assumptions about human behaviour.

explanation: Different responses by groups show that economic behaviour is shaped by people and circumstances. This variation is a feature of studying society and helps explain why economic relationships may be less controlled than relationships in laboratory sciences.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: An economist has strong evidence that a tax reduces pollution. Can the evidence alone prove that the tax should be introduced?

options.label: A
options.text: No; choosing policy also requires value judgements.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; measured effects determine what policy is fairest.

options.label: C
options.text: No; economic observations cannot support positive policy claims.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes; fairness follows solely from measured pollution levels.

explanation: Evidence can support the positive claim about the tax's effect on pollution. Whether the policy should be introduced depends additionally on priorities, costs and values, so factual evidence alone cannot settle the normative judgement.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A study estimates that a rise in advertising increases sales, assuming product quality and competitors' prices do not change. What is the main purpose of these assumptions?

options.label: A
options.text: To turn a causal relationship into a value judgement.

options.label: B
options.text: To establish that all productive inputs can change.

options.label: C
options.text: To establish permanent stability of competitors’ prices.

options.label: D
options.text: To isolate advertising’s effect from other sales determinants.

explanation: Holding product quality and competitors' prices constant is a ceteris paribus device. It makes it easier to identify the separate effect of advertising on sales rather than mixing several changes together.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm can change its workforce and machinery, but a new production technology is not yet available. Which time period is most consistent with this description?

options.label: A
options.text: The time period cannot be classified because no number of years is given

options.label: B
options.text: The long run

options.label: C
options.text: The short run

options.label: D
options.text: The very long run

explanation: The firm can vary all factor inputs, which places the decision in the long run. A change in wider key conditions such as technology is not required until the very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement is normative even though it does not use the word 'should'?

options.label: A
options.text: The unemployment rate is 7%.

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment rose by one percentage point.

options.label: C
options.text: A 7% unemployment rate is intolerably high.

options.label: D
options.text: The labour force contains 2 million people.

explanation: 'Intolerably high' expresses a judgement about an acceptable level of unemployment. A normative statement can contain value-laden language without explicitly using the word 'should'.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A researcher compares two countries but cannot hold their institutions, expectations and cultures constant. What methodological problem does this create?

options.label: A
options.text: It turns every observation into a value judgement.

options.label: B
options.text: It establishes that every factor input is variable.

options.label: C
options.text: It prevents the collection of any numerical observations.

options.label: D
options.text: It complicates isolating a single cause’s effect.

explanation: Because several social and institutional influences differ at the same time, it is harder to isolate causation. This is a common challenge in a social science where controlled laboratory conditions are often unavailable.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A restaurant can change staffing immediately, replace all kitchen equipment within a year, and only much later adopt a new industry-wide technology. Which change marks entry into the long run?

options.label: A
options.text: When every factor input can be varied.

options.label: B
options.text: When precisely twelve calendar months have elapsed.

options.label: C
options.text: When staffing can first be varied independently.

options.label: D
options.text: When industry-wide technology can first be changed.

explanation: The long run begins when all factor inputs can be changed. The ability to alter staffing alone is consistent with the short run, while a broader technological change is characteristic of the very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt:
Which row correctly classifies the statements?
| Statement | Text |
| 1 | Lower inflation is better than faster growth. |
| 2 | Real output increased by 2% last year. |
| 3 | The current distribution of income is unjust. |

options.label: A
options.text: 1 positive, 2 normative, 3 positive

options.label: B
options.text: 1 normative, 2 normative, 3 positive

options.label: C
options.text: 1 positive, 2 positive, 3 normative

options.label: D
options.text: 1 normative, 2 positive, 3 normative

explanation: Statement 1 makes a judgement about what is 'better', statement 2 is a testable claim about measured output, and statement 3 says a distribution is 'unjust'. The correct sequence is therefore normative, positive, normative.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An analyst examines the effect of higher interest rates on saving while income is also rising rapidly. Why does this weaken a ceteris paribus analysis of the interest-rate effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Rising income turns positive forecasts into normative claims.

options.label: B
options.text: Rising income prevents the collection of interest-rate data.

options.label: C
options.text: Rising income satisfies the assumption of unchanged conditions.

options.label: D
options.text: Income changes confound the isolated interest-rate effect.

explanation: If income changes at the same time, one of the other determinants has not been held constant. Any observed change in saving may reflect the interest-rate change, the income change or both, so the isolated causal effect is less clear.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A shipyard cannot expand its dry dock this year, although it can alter overtime hours. What is the most appropriate economic time period for this year's decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Short run

options.label: B
options.text: No time period because physical capital is involved

options.label: C
options.text: Long run

options.label: D
options.text: Very long run

explanation: At least one important factor input remains fixed while another can be varied. That is the defining condition of the short run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is the strongest limitation of treating an economic model as an exact description of reality?

options.label: A
options.text: Models cannot include quantities or measurable variables.

options.label: B
options.text: Models deliberately simplify behaviour and market conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: Models necessarily express judgements about policy fairness.

options.label: D
options.text: Models must exclude assumptions about economic behaviour.

explanation: Models are useful because they simplify complex economic relationships. The same simplification means they should not be treated as exact replicas of reality, especially when assumptions or human behaviour differ from the model.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A minister says, 'A higher fuel tax will cut fuel use, so it is the best policy.' Which part is normative?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim that fuel use can change

options.label: B
options.text: The claim that the tax is the best policy

options.label: C
options.text: The whole statement simply because a minister said it

options.label: D
options.text: The claim that the tax is higher

explanation: The predicted effect on fuel use is a positive claim that can be tested. Calling the tax the 'best' policy requires a judgement about objectives and trade-offs, making that part normative.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A policy has been in place for two years. Why is this information alone insufficient to decide whether the economy is in the long run?

options.label: A
options.text: The long run starts when every price stays constant.

options.label: B
options.text: The long run ends after two calendar years.

options.label: C
options.text: The long run depends on which inputs can adjust.

options.label: D
options.text: The long run applies only to normative policy judgements.

explanation: Short run and long run are economic concepts defined by adjustment possibilities. Two years may be enough for all inputs to vary in one context but not in another.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which application uses ceteris paribus correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: Change wages and productivity, attributing all effects to wages.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume higher wages are fair because employment changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Change wages while holding other demand determinants constant.

options.label: D
options.text: Define the long run by whether wages stay unchanged.

explanation: Ceteris paribus isolates one relationship by holding other relevant influences constant. Simultaneously changing several determinants makes it impossible to identify the separate effect of the wage change.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement is positive despite being disputed by economists?

options.label: A
options.text: The central bank ought to avoid higher interest rates.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher policy rates will reduce investment next year.

options.label: C
options.text: Stable investment is more important than stable prices.

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing investment would be an undesirable policy outcome.

explanation: A positive statement is defined by being testable in principle, not by all economists agreeing that it is true. The predicted change in investment can be compared with evidence; the other statements express values or priorities.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economic forecast is wrong even though its calculations were accurate. Which explanation is most consistent with economics being a social science?

options.label: A
options.text: Economic outcomes cannot be measured using numerical data.

options.label: B
options.text: Social-science models cannot use mathematical or statistical methods.

options.label: C
options.text: Behaviour changed in ways the model did not anticipate.

options.label: D
options.text: An inaccurate prediction necessarily expresses a value judgement.

explanation: Economic forecasts depend on assumptions about behaviour and circumstances. People may respond differently from the model's expectation, so a forecast can be wrong even when its arithmetic is correct.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A factory can alter every factor input but government safety rules and available production technology remain unchanged. Which time period is being described?

options.label: A
options.text: Long run

options.label: B
options.text: Short run

options.label: C
options.text: Very long run

options.label: D

explanation: All factor inputs can vary, satisfying the long-run definition. The wider conditions mentioned remain fixed, so the description does not require the very long run.

prompt: A statement says, 'A minimum wage increases labour costs and therefore ought to be removed.' Which classification is most accurate?

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: The effect on labour costs is a testable positive claim. The conclusion that the policy 'ought to be removed' is a value judgement, so the statement combines both types.

prompt: A model predicts the effect of a price change while holding income constant. Income actually falls at the same time. What has happened to the model's ceteris paribus condition?

options.label: A
options.text: It has changed the analysis automatically into the very long run.

options.label: B
options.text: It has been strengthened because two variables moved.

options.label: C
options.text: It has been violated because another relevant variable changed.

options.label: D
options.text: It has turned the prediction into a normative statement.

explanation: The prediction isolates the price change only if other relevant influences such as income remain constant. Since income also changed, the ceteris paribus condition no longer holds.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A farmer can vary fertiliser and labour this season but cannot change the amount of land used. Which economic time period best describes the decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Long run

options.label: B
options.text: Very long run

options.label: C
options.text: Short run

options.label: D

reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Two economists observe the same data but recommend different policies because they give different importance to equality and efficiency. What best explains their disagreement?

options.label: A
options.text: Disagreement removes economics from the study of human behaviour.

options.label: B
options.text: Disagreement establishes that factual economic claims cannot be tested.

options.label: C
options.text: Different recommendations establish that one economist ignored the evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Different value judgements can accompany the same factual evidence.

explanation: Economists can agree on positive evidence yet differ over objectives, priorities and values. This is consistent with economics as a social science in which policy decisions often combine factual analysis with normative judgement.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement about a prediction is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Numbers turn every forecast into a normative statement.

options.label: B
options.text: Future evidence can test a positive forecast.

options.label: C
options.text: Future events make every forecast a value judgement.

options.label: D
options.text: Universal agreement makes every forecast a positive statement.

explanation: Positive statements include testable predictions as well as descriptions of past or present facts. The key distinction is whether the claim can be confronted with evidence, not whether the event has already occurred.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A manufacturer is considering a period in which its factory size, machinery and labour can all be adjusted. Which feature makes this long-run analysis rather than short-run analysis?

options.label: A
options.text: The decision involves a manufacturer

options.label: B
options.text: No factor input is fixed

options.label: C
options.text: The period is longer than twelve months

options.label: D

explanation: The long run is defined by all factor inputs being variable. The type of firm and the number of calendar months do not by themselves determine the economic time period.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A researcher wants to know the effect of education on earnings. Which approach most closely follows ceteris paribus reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: Allow every determinant of earnings to change and attribute all differences to education.

options.label: B
options.text: Use only evidence from periods in which technology changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Assume education is desirable and then collect no data.

options.label: D
options.text: Compare outcomes while attempting to control for other influences on earnings.

explanation: Ceteris paribus reasoning tries to isolate the influence of education by controlling other relevant determinants. If many influences vary freely, observed earnings differences cannot be attributed to education alone.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which claim about poverty depends on a judgement about social success?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower poverty makes a society more successful.

options.label: B
options.text: A lower threshold reduces measured poverty in this dataset.

options.label: C
options.text: The poverty rate fell by three percentage points.

options.label: D
options.text: The poverty measure uses observed household income data.

explanation: Calling one society 'more successful' requires a judgement about what counts as success. The other statements are factual or testable relationships.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which observation is most relevant to economics being a social science rather than a laboratory science?

options.label: A
options.text: Economists can express relationships using mathematical equations.

options.label: B
options.text: Researchers can present numerical observations in tables.

options.label: C
options.text: People change decisions as policies and expectations change.

options.label: D
options.text: Economists can measure observations as percentage changes.

explanation: The distinctive issue is that the subjects of study are people and institutions whose behaviour can change. Equations, tables and percentages are methods that can be used in both social and natural sciences.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A company can change staffing now, expand its building later, and eventually benefit from a new technology that changes the industry's production methods. Which stage is the very long run?

options.label: A
options.text: The stage when the new technology can also change

options.label: B
options.text: The stage when the building can change but technology cannot

options.label: C
options.text: Every stage after one calendar year

options.label: D
options.text: The stage when staffing alone changes

explanation: The very long run allows not only all factor inputs but also wider key inputs such as technology to vary. Changing staffing alone is short run; varying all factor inputs with technology fixed is long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which claim about retirement age is a testable prediction rather than a value judgement?

options.label: A
options.text: A higher retirement age should be rejected.

options.label: B
options.text: A higher retirement age may expand labour supply.

options.label: C
options.text: A higher retirement age treats older workers unfairly.

options.label: D
options.text: A higher retirement age improves society’s moral character.

explanation: The predicted change in labour-force size is a testable causal claim, so it is positive. The other statements express fairness, desirability or what ought to happen.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economist says that a tax rise reduces spending, ceteris paribus. Which interpretation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Other spending determinants are assumed unchanged for this comparison.

options.label: B
options.text: Other spending determinants can never change in observed reality.

options.label: C
options.text: Assumptions turn the tax prediction into a value judgement.

options.label: D
options.text: Every productive input must become variable before the economist can analyse any change in household spending.

explanation: Ceteris paribus is a simplifying conditional assumption. It does not assert that other variables never change; it asks what would happen if they were held constant while the tax changes.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm reaches a point where all factor inputs can be varied, but a change in environmental regulation occurs only later. Which sequence is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Short run first, short run later

options.label: B
options.text: Very long run first, long run later

options.label: C
options.text: Very long run first, short run later

options.label: D
options.text: Long run first, very long run later

explanation: The ability to vary all factor inputs defines the long run. A later change in a wider key condition such as government regulation is characteristic of the very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Three claims are made about a subsidy. Which claim is normative?

options.label: A
options.text: The subsidy can change firms' production costs.

options.label: B
options.text: The subsidy is an unjustified use of taxpayers' money.

options.label: C
options.text: The subsidy costs the government $40 million a year.

options.label: D

explanation: Describing the subsidy as 'unjustified' expresses a value judgement. The other claims concern measurable facts or testable economic effects.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A market study holds consumer income constant but allows tastes and the prices of related goods to change. Can it isolate the effect of the product's own price on demand?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because holding any one variable constant is sufficient for ceteris paribus.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because tastes are normative and therefore irrelevant.

options.label: C
options.text: Not reliably, because ceteris paribus requires the product's own price to stay fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: Not reliably, because other determinants of demand are also changing.

explanation: To isolate the effect of one variable, other relevant determinants must be held constant. If tastes and related-goods prices change, the observed demand change may reflect several causes.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A researcher finds a strong correlation between two economic variables. Why should this not automatically be treated as proof that one causes the other?

options.label: A
options.text: Numerical measurement is unavailable for social-science observations.

options.label: B
options.text: Causation occurs only when every productive input can change.

options.label: C
options.text: A third influence may affect both variables.

options.label: D
options.text: Correlation expresses a judgement about socially desirable outcomes.

explanation: In social data, several influences may change together, so a correlation can arise without a direct causal link. Establishing causation requires careful reasoning about other possible influences and assumptions.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which is a normative statement about inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: A higher inflation rate reduces the purchasing power of a fixed money income.

options.label: B
options.text: The inflation rate is measured using a price index.

options.label: C
options.text: Price stability deserves a higher priority than faster economic growth.

options.label: D
options.text: The inflation rate fell by two percentage points.

explanation: Giving one objective a 'higher priority' expresses a value judgement. The remaining statements are factual or testable claims.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why can economics use mathematical and statistical methods while still be classified as a social science?

options.label: A
options.text: Numbers determine whether a subject is a natural science.

options.label: B
options.text: Social science excludes equations and statistical analysis of evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: Only judgements about fairness qualify as social-science investigations.

options.label: D
options.text: Human behaviour remains the subject of quantitative analysis.

explanation: A field is classified by the subject matter it investigates, not by whether it uses numbers. Economics studies human behaviour, choices and institutions, while mathematical and statistical methods can still be used to analyse that social evidence.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economic theory predicts a result only under specified assumptions. What is the most appropriate way to interpret the theory?

options.label: A
options.text: A value judgement that cannot face empirical testing.

options.label: B
options.text: Evidence that assumptions have no analytical purpose.

options.label: C
options.text: A guaranteed relationship under every conceivable condition.

options.label: D
options.text: A conditional explanation dependent on its assumptions.

explanation: Economic models and theories simplify reality and generate conditional predictions. Their usefulness depends partly on whether the assumptions are reasonable for the situation being analysed.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which event is most clearly associated with moving from the long run to the very long run?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Adopting technology that changes available production methods.

options.label: D

explanation: The very long run allows wider key inputs such as technology to change. Hiring workers with fixed capacity is short-run adjustment, while changing all factor inputs within existing technology is long-run adjustment.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt:
Which row correctly classifies the two claims?
| Claim | Text |

prompt: A firm can change all factor inputs within eighteen months, while another needs four years. What follows?

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: Every firm reaches the very long run before the long run.

options.label: D
options.text: Variable inputs mean the first firm has no short run.

explanation: The long run begins when all factor inputs can be changed, and the time needed to reach that point varies by firm and industry. There is no fixed calendar rule.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement best explains why normative economics is relevant to government policy?

options.label: A

explanation: Government policy involves deciding which objectives and outcomes are preferable, not only predicting effects. These choices often require value judgements, although positive evidence can inform them.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An analyst says that a price rise will reduce sales only if other determinants of demand are unchanged. Which word best describes this condition?

prompt: A public transport company can change every factor input, and new autonomous-vehicle technology is also available. Which is the broadest relevant time period?

options.label: A
options.text: Long run only

options.label: B
options.text: A fixed one-year period

options.label: C
options.text: Very long run

options.label: D
options.text: Short run

explanation: Because all factor inputs and a wider key input - technology - can change, the description fits the very long run. Long-run analysis alone does not require technology to change.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Firm X can change all its factor inputs after eight months. Firm Y can change only some inputs after eighteen months. Which conclusion is valid?

options.label: A
options.text: Y’s very long run necessarily begins before X’s long run.

options.label: B
options.text: Both firms enter the long run after twelve calendar months.

options.label: C
options.text: X remains in the short run until twelve months elapse.

options.label: D
options.text: X reaches the long run while Y remains short-run constrained.

explanation: Economic time periods are defined by adjustment possibilities rather than clock time. X can vary all factor inputs after eight months, so it may have reached the long run; Y still has fixed inputs after eighteen months, so it can remain in the short run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A study finds that sales rose after a price cut, but consumer income and a competitor's price also changed. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: The price cut must account for the entire observed increase in sales, irrespective of simultaneous income and competitor-price changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Other changes must be accounted for to isolate the price effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Several changing variables make the observed sales figures normative.

options.label: D
options.text: Simultaneous changes satisfy the assumption of unchanged demand determinants.

explanation: A ceteris paribus inference requires other relevant determinants to remain constant. Since income and a competitor's price also changed, the observed sales increase cannot confidently be attributed entirely to the product's own price cut.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement is positive even though it includes the word 'should'?

options.label: A

options.text: Five per cent unemployment should be regarded as unacceptable.

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment should receive priority over income-tax reductions.

explanation: Here 'should fall' is used as a prediction about a measurable future outcome, not as a recommendation about what ought to happen. The other options use 'should' to express values, priorities or acceptable outcomes, making them normative.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A firm can vary all current factor inputs, but a major change in regulation next year will alter which production methods are legally permitted. How should the two stages be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: Current inputs: long run; changed rules: very long run.

options.label: B
options.text: Current inputs: long run; changed rules: short run.

options.label: C
options.text: Current inputs: short run; changed rules: long run.

options.label: D
options.text: Current inputs: very long run; changed rules: short run.

explanation: The current stage is long run because all factor inputs can vary. Once a wider key condition such as government regulation also changes, the analysis extends to the very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economist uses a model that accurately predicts average behaviour but performs poorly for some individuals. Which judgement is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Imperfect individual forecasts make every aggregate prediction useless.

options.label: B
options.text: Useful average predictions can coexist with individual limitations.

options.label: C
options.text: Inaccurate individual predictions convert measured effects into value judgements.

options.label: D
options.text: Accurate average predictions establish identical behaviour across all individuals.

explanation: A social-science model can capture broad patterns without predicting every person's behaviour exactly. Its usefulness should be judged against its purpose and assumptions, while recognising the limitation created by variation among individuals.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: An economist says, 'The policy will increase average income, therefore it is the fairest policy.' What is the methodological error?

options.label: A
options.text: An income prediction is treated as proof of fairness.

options.label: B
options.text: A fairness judgement disproves every prediction about average income.

options.label: C
options.text: A fairness judgement is necessarily more testable than measured income.

options.label: D
options.text: An income prediction cannot be tested using observed economic data.

explanation: Whether average income rises is a positive, testable issue. Whether the policy is fairest requires a value judgement and may depend on distribution and priorities, so the positive prediction does not by itself establish the normative conclusion.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which sequence of changes best represents movement through the short run, long run and very long run?

options.label: A
options.text: Technology and production methods vary → every input becomes fixed → some inputs become variable again.

options.label: B
options.text: All inputs fixed → technology varies → only labour variable.

options.label: C
options.text: All inputs variable → some inputs variable → all inputs fixed.

options.label: D

explanation: The short run allows some but not all factor inputs to change. In the long run all factor inputs can vary, while the very long run extends adjustment to wider key conditions such as technology and regulation.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economist estimates the effect of a tax on consumption by comparing periods before and after the tax. Advertising also increased sharply after the tax. Which condition would most improve the ceteris paribus interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Evidence that voters approve of the tax increase.

options.label: B
options.text: Evidence that advertising’s effect has been controlled for.

options.label: C
options.text: Evidence that taxpayers consider the tax increase fair.

options.label: D
options.text: Evidence that variables are expressed in monetary units.

explanation: Advertising is another influence on consumption. To isolate the tax effect, the analyst needs to hold that influence constant conceptually or control for it in the analysis; political popularity and fairness are unrelated to the ceteris paribus requirement.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consider two claims: (1) a higher tax rate will reduce disposable income; (2) reducing disposable income is unacceptable. Which statement about them is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Claim 1 is positive and claim 2 is normative.

options.label: B
options.text: Claim 1 is normative and claim 2 is positive.

options.label: C
options.text: Both claims are normative because taxes involve government policy.

options.label: D
options.text: Both claims are positive because both concern income.

explanation: Claim 1 is a testable causal statement about income. Claim 2 evaluates the outcome as 'unacceptable', which requires a value judgement, so it is normative.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A construction firm can vary labour and materials but cannot alter its heavy equipment. Later it can alter all three, and later still new building technology becomes available. Which classification is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: First short run, then long run, then very long run

options.text: All three stages are long run because output can change

options.label: D

explanation: The first stage has at least one fixed factor input, so it is short run. The second allows all factor inputs to vary, so it is long run. The final stage also changes technology, a wider key input, so it is very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A model claims X causes Y, ceteris paribus. Which finding most directly challenges the model's isolated causal test rather than the logical meaning of ceteris paribus?

options.label: A
options.text: Other determinants are explicitly held constant in the model.

options.label: B
options.text: The model predicts outcomes without judging their desirability.

options.label: C
options.text: The model describes a relationship using words rather than equations.

options.label: D
options.text: A third determinant changes systematically with the studied variable.

explanation: If another determinant changes systematically with X, observed changes in Y may reflect both influences, undermining isolation of X's effect. The existence of the ceteris paribus assumption itself is not a flaw; the issue is whether the empirical setting approximates it.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can two well-informed economists make different forecasts from the same current data?

options.label: A
options.text: Different behavioural assumptions can produce different forecasts.

options.label: B
options.text: Models cannot be used to interpret current economic observations.

options.label: C
options.text: Current observations determine future outcomes without any uncertainty.

options.label: D
options.text: Only one forecast can qualify as a positive statement.

explanation: Forecasts depend not only on current data but also on assumptions about behavioural responses and future conditions. Different reasonable assumptions can therefore produce different positive forecasts in a social science.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A firm can vary every factor input, but consumer preferences, technology and government rules are treated as fixed. Which classification is most precise?

options.label: A
options.text: Unclassifiable because consumer preferences are specified.

options.label: B
options.text: Long run with technology and wider conditions fixed.

options.label: C
options.text: Short run because every productive input stays fixed.

explanation: All factor inputs are variable, so the firm is in the long run. The very long run would also allow wider key conditions, such as technology or government rules, to change.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An analyst wants to estimate the effect of a change in working hours on output. Productivity-enhancing software is introduced at the same time. What is the best methodological response?

options.label: A

options.text: Treat technological change as a normative output measure.

options.text: Treat simultaneous software changes as unchanged productive conditions.

explanation: The software is another plausible determinant of output. A ceteris paribus analysis of working hours must hold such influences constant or otherwise account for them before making a causal attribution.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm has reached the long run. Which additional change would most clearly move the analysis into the very long run?

options.label: A
options.text: Changing quantities of inputs within existing production methods.

options.label: B
options.text: Changing plant capacity within existing production methods.

options.label: C
options.text: Changing employee numbers within existing production methods.

options.label: D
options.text: Changing available technology and production methods.

explanation: Long-run analysis already allows all factor inputs to vary. A change in technology is a wider key change and therefore provides the clearest move into very-long-run analysis.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A newspaper reports: 'Inflation fell to 2%, proving that the central bank made the right decision.' Which part cannot be established by the inflation figure alone?

options.label: A
options.text: That the statement contains a numerical claim

options.label: C
options.text: That the decision was right

options.label: D

explanation: The 2% figure is positive information. Whether the central bank's decision was 'right' depends on objectives, alternatives and values, so that normative judgement cannot be proved by the inflation figure alone.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A researcher holds all observed determinants constant but an unobserved influence changes with the variable being studied. What is the main implication for ceteris paribus reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: Only observed determinants matter when testing isolated causal effects.

options.label: B
options.text: Unobserved influences make every causal prediction a value judgement.

options.text: Unobserved influences establish that all inputs have become variable.

options.label: D
options.text: Unobserved influences can still confound the estimated effect.

explanation: Ceteris paribus requires other relevant influences to be unchanged, whether or not they are easily observed. If an unobserved determinant changes systematically, it can contaminate the apparent effect of the variable under study.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which consideration best explains why a very long-run forecast may be less certain than a short-run conditional analysis?

options.label: A
options.text: More fundamental conditions may change over a longer horizon.

options.label: B
options.text: Short-run predictions require no assumptions about underlying behaviour.

options.label: C
options.text: Longer horizons turn judgements of fairness into measurable facts.

options.label: D
options.text: Longer horizons prevent changes in productive inputs and technology.

explanation: Very-long-run analysis admits changes in a wider set of key influences, increasing the number of conditions that may differ from today's assumptions. This can make forecasts more uncertain even though the concept itself is not defined by a fixed number of years.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement is positive but could still depend on a ceteris paribus assumption?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower prices are fairer for all consumers.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher prices treat low-income consumers unfairly.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher prices reduce sales, other things equal.

options.label: D
options.text: Government should prevent higher prices for consumers.

explanation: Option C is a testable conditional claim and is therefore positive. Its prediction explicitly depends on holding other determinants constant, showing that positive analysis can use ceteris paribus assumptions.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economist concludes from a controlled model that a policy will raise output. Which further step is needed before concluding that the policy ought to be adopted?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the output prediction until it becomes certain.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume other policy options have no economic effects.

options.label: C
options.text: Postpone value judgements until every productive input can vary.

options.label: D
options.text: Assess other effects and judgements about desirable outcomes.

explanation: A model can provide positive analysis of likely effects, but a policy recommendation also requires judgement about objectives, trade-offs and priorities. The social-science analysis does not automatically turn a predicted output gain into a complete normative case for adoption.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A company can change its plant size but not the industry technology it uses. A rival can change plant size and adopt a new technology. Both firms can vary all factor inputs. Which classification is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: First: very long run; second: long run.

options.label: B
options.text: First: long run; second: very long run.

options.label: C
options.text: First: very long run; second: short run.

options.label: D
options.text: First: short run; second: short run.

explanation: Changing all factor inputs, including plant size, is consistent with the long run. When technology can also change, the range of adjustment extends into the very long run.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A claim says that a tax 'will probably reduce consumption by 4%'. Which feature determines whether it is positive or normative?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether evidence could test the predicted outcome.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether voters consider the predicted outcome desirable.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether the predicted outcome is morally acceptable.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether taxpayers consider the proposed policy fair.

explanation: Uncertainty does not make a statement normative. A probabilistic forecast about a measurable 4% change can still be positive because evidence can be used to assess it.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A model compares the effect of two policies while assuming the same external conditions for each. Why is this ceteris paribus assumption useful?

options.label: A
options.text: It establishes identical desirability of the two policies.

options.label: B
options.text: It requires unchanged external conditions forever in reality.

options.label: C
options.text: It isolates differences attributable to the two policies.

options.label: D
options.text: It establishes that every external condition can vary.

explanation: Holding external conditions constant creates a common basis for comparison. Differences in the modelled outcomes can then be linked more clearly to the policies rather than to different background conditions.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which situation most clearly shows why the same event can have different short-run and long-run effects?

options.label: A
options.text: A researcher repeats the same measured price observation.

options.label: B
options.text: Fixed capacity later becomes adjustable productive capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: Every productive condition stays permanently fixed by assumption.

options.label: D
options.text: An observer changes a judgement about policy fairness.

explanation: The time dimension matters because adjustment possibilities expand. A firm may be constrained by fixed inputs in the short run but able to change all factor inputs in the long run, leading to different responses to the same event.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economist states, 'The evidence suggests the policy raises employment, but whether the policy is desirable depends on its other effects.' What methodological distinction is being recognised?

options.label: A
options.text: Policy assessment requires every productive input to become variable.

options.label: B
options.text: Observed effects make facts and fairness judgements identical.

options.label: C
options.text: Evidence about effects does not alone establish desirability.

options.label: D
options.text: Measured employment changes necessarily express judgements about fairness.

explanation: The employment effect is a positive, evidence-based issue. Deciding whether the policy is desirable requires weighing other consequences and values, which is normative.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A researcher deliberately simplifies a complex market to three variables and then tests the model against data. Which description best fits this method?

options.label: A
options.text: Model use prevents the investigation from being economic analysis.

options.label: B
options.text: Variable selection makes every conclusion a judgement about fairness.

options.label: C
options.text: One matching dataset proves the model holds under all conditions.

options.label: D
options.text: Evidence is used to assess a simplified economic model.

explanation: Economists often simplify complex reality into models and compare their implications with evidence. A good fit can support a model, but it does not remove the model's assumptions or prove it universally true.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.1 economics as a social science | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A firm can hire or release labour immediately, can vary all factor inputs after two years, and may face new technology and regulation after five years. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Any variable input ends the short run for every firm.

options.label: B
options.text: Variable labour alone starts the very long run for every firm.

options.label: C
options.text: Two and five years define identical time periods for every firm.

options.label: D
options.text: Available adjustments determine economic periods for this particular firm.

explanation: The scenario illustrates short-, long- and very-long-run adjustment, but the key is what can change at each stage. The numerical durations are context-specific rather than universal definitions.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement is normative even if every factual claim within it is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The tax generated more revenue than last year.

options.label: B
options.text: The tax is the government’s most responsible policy.

options.label: C
options.text: The tax generated two billion dollars last year.

options.label: D
options.text: The tax receipts appear in published government accounts.

explanation: The factual premise can be verified, but calling the policy 'most responsible' is a value judgement. Accurate facts can inform a normative statement without converting the judgement itself into a positive fact.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.2 positive and normative statements (the distinction between facts and value judgements) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A ceteris paribus model predicts that changing X changes Y. In reality X changes, Y does not, and another determinant of Y changes in the opposite direction. What is the most careful conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: Unchanged Y conclusively disproves every isolated effect of X.

options.label: B
options.text: The other determinant has no relevance outside the model.

options.label: C
options.text: Changed conditions prevent this observation isolating X’s effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Changed conditions turn the causal relationship into a value judgement.

explanation: The model's prediction is conditional on other determinants remaining equal. An offsetting change in another determinant means the real-world observation is not a clean test of the isolated X-to-Y relationship.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.3 meaning of the term ceteris paribus | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which comparison between the long run and very long run is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Long run: fixed calendar dates; very long run: later dates.

options.label: B
options.text: Long run: technology variable; very long run: only labour variable.

options.label: C
options.text: Long run: all inputs variable; very long run: wider conditions variable.

options.label: D
options.text: Long run: some productive inputs remain fixed; very long run: every productive input becomes fixed again.

explanation: The long run is defined by all factor inputs being variable. The very long run extends the scope of change to wider key influences such as technology, regulation and social considerations.
reference: 1.2 Economic methodology | 1.2.4 importance of the time period (short run, long run, very long run) | AO2 Analysis
